snippet.title: How One Lawsuit Destroyed America's Biggest Trucks
snippet.description: For most of the 1950s and 60s, if you stood beside an open pit anywhere in America and watched the rock come out, better than one in two of the giant trucks doing the hauling carried a single name on the nose: Euclid. From a factory in a small town outside Cleveland, Ohio, one company invented the off-highway hauler and then dominated it completely. Euclid didn't just lead the market — it owned it, out-building every rival in the country combined. Its trucks built the interstates, raised the great dams, and tore open the strip mines that rebuilt the nation after the war. The name became a generic word in the pits; men didn't say they drove a hauler, they said they drove a "Euc." But fast forward past 1968, and it's gone. General Motors, which had bought Euclid to make it invincible, is ordered to break it apart. The company is sold off, barred from its own market, and stripped of its own name. Now, there is a simple villain in this story. Its name is the United States government, and the antitrust lawyer who decided Euclid had simply become too successful. But the truth is more complicated — and more damning. Because nobody ever beat Euclid by building a better truck. It was undone in a courtroom, split in two, and slowly scattered until the biggest trucks in America carried names from Sweden and Japan. This is how one lawsuit destroyed America's biggest trucks. snippet.title: The Lawsuit That Destroyed Smartphones
snippet.description:
At the start of the 2010s, Apple and Samsung entered the courtroom in a battle over the DNA of their most well-known products, the iPhone and Galaxy lineup. This wasn’t just a war over trademarks or patents, but a clash for the design of the modern world. Combined, these two devices have sold over six billion units since their launch in the late 2000s, generating upwards of $3.7 trillion in revenue. For perspective, that is higher than the nominal economic output of France, Canada, and Russia. 

As massive as those figures are, once those two giants walked out of the room, the course of the smartphone industry would change fundamentally, but in a way that went over our heads for years.

As the company built up to the release of the iPhone in 2007, Apple filed a handful of patents centred on the device's basic shape in January of that year. These patents would include essential features we take for granted nowadays, such as rubber-band scrolling and pinch-to-zoom. While we were promised the future of smartphones would look more like they came out of Star Wars or Cyberpunk, what we ultimately got were the simple, plain slabs that could slip into our pockets and vibrate for notifications. 

But to understand why the phones of today are the same design copied and pasted, we have to take a trip down memory lane, back to the boardroom meeting that would change everything. We’ll get to that in a few minutes, but first, let’s take a look at the starting point of this conflict– the moment Samsung made a pivot so radical it made Steve Jobs boil.

snippet.title: Hulk Hogan vs Gawker: The Lawsuit That Destroyed a Media Empire
snippet.description:
When a professional wrestler's private life collided with a billionaire's vendetta and a media empire's ruthless pursuit of clicks, the result was one of the most explosive legal battles in modern media history. This is the incredible true story of how Hulk Hogan's leaked sex tape became the weapon that brought down Gawker Media – a digital empire worth over $400 million that seemed untouchable. What started as gossip blog coverage spiraled into a courtroom showdown that would rewrite the rules of privacy, press freedom, and revenge in the internet age.

Behind the scenes, billionaire Peter Thiel was secretly funding Hogan's legal war against Gawker, seeking payback for being publicly outed years earlier on the site. Gawker's "radical transparency" philosophy – their willingness to publish what others wouldn't dare – had made them powerful enemies along the way. When the dust settled, this wasn't just about a wrestler's dignity or a media company's destruction – it was about the dangerous intersection of unlimited wealth, personal vendettas, and the power to silence the press. The verdict that emerged would send shockwaves through Silicon Valley and fundamentally change how we think about privacy versus public interest in the digital era.

snippet.title: The Lawsuit That Broke Up the Most Powerful Company in America
snippet.description:
In the early 1900s, one company controlled nearly all of the oil refining in the United States. Standard Oil, founded by John D. Rockefeller, had become so powerful that it dominated pipelines, refineries, transportation, and fuel prices across the country.

But in 1911, the United States government filed a lawsuit that would change American business forever. The Supreme Court ruled that Standard Oil was an illegal monopoly and ordered it to be broken into more than 30 separate companies — many of which would later become Exxon, Mobil, Chevron, and other major oil companies that still exist today.

This case didn’t just break up one company. It created the foundation for modern antitrust law and changed how governments regulate powerful corporations to this day.

This is the story of the lawsuit that broke up the most powerful company in America.

Valve will win the UK lawsuit because allowing the case to proceed does not mean Steam has been found to have broken competition law. It only means the claim met the minimum threshold to be heard. Under UK competition law, even a dominant company is not acting unlawfully unless there is clear abuse of that position. Valve can argue that Steam’s size is the result of competitive success and consumer preference, not exclusionary conduct, and that developers voluntarily choose to use the platform because of the value it provides.

In addition, Valve is likely to argue that the practices challenged in the UK lawsuit, such as platform commissions and contractual terms, are common across the digital games industry and therefore not inherently anti-competitive. A key weakness for the claimants is proving direct consumer harm. Game prices are set by publishers, not Steam, and price levels are influenced by many factors beyond Valve’s fees. If the court finds the economic evidence speculative or unconvincing, it may conclude that Steam’s conduct does not amount to an abuse of dominance, strengthening Valve’s chances of winning the case.

In addition, Valve is likely to argue that the practices challenged in the UK lawsuit, such as platform commissions and contractual terms, are common across the digital games industry and therefore not inherently anti-competitive. A key weakness for the claimants is proving direct consumer harm. Game prices are set by publishers, not Steam, and price levels are influenced by many factors beyond Valve’s fees. If the court finds the economic evidence speculative or unconvincing, it may conclude that Steam’s conduct does not amount to an abuse of dominance, strengthening Valve’s chances of winning the case.

snippet.title: Greedy Empire Exposed How a Class Action Lawsuit Destroyed the Company That Exploited Workers (S5E9)
snippet.description: This gripping true-crime business documentary uncovers the shocking downfall of BrighTex, a once-celebrated corporation that built its empire on exploitation, wage theft, and worker abuse. What began as whispers on the factory floor turned into a historic class action lawsuit that shook the company to its core. In this in-depth investigation, we reveal how ordinary workers—many immigrants and underpaid laborers—found the courage to unite, expose systemic exploitation, and take on powerful executives who thought they were untouchable. Through emotional testimonies, leaked emails, and courtroom drama, you’ll witness how greed, corruption, and disregard for human life led to a spectacular corporate collapse. This story is more than just a scandal—it’s a lesson in courage, solidarity, and the unstoppable power of collective action. Perfect for fans of business documentaries, corporate crime stories, and labor rights exposés, this video explores not only the rise and fall of BrighTex but also what it means for workers everywhere. If you’ve ever wondered how much suffering hides behind cheap products, or how far corporations will go for profit, this documentary will open your eyes. Watch until the end to learn how ordinary people turned fear into power—and how their victory sent shockwaves across industries worldwide.
